reception.text: Western settlers and their representatives protested that good-faith homesteaders were being shut out of land they were entitled to claim.
Coal and railroad interests objected to losing cheap acquisition of coal land.

Constitutional critics charged that only Congress could dispose of the public domain and that the President was legislating by decree; Roosevelt later recalled 'a great clamor that I was usurping legislative power.'
reception.source: Theodore Roosevelt, An Autobiography (1913), ch. X

political_impact.text: The withdrawals were carried out as departmental orders from the Interior Department to the General Land Office; Secretary Hitchcock told Roosevelt no formal executive order was needed.
political_impact.source: Hitchcock to Roosevelt, Dec. 17, 1906, Theodore Roosevelt Papers, LOC, reel 70

political_impact.text: By June 30, 1907 the General Land Office counted 66,716,240 acres withdrawn, 8,524,800 already restored and 58,191,440 still withdrawn.
political_impact.source: Report of the Commissioner of the General Land Office, FY1907, pp. 187–188

political_impact.text: The Geological Survey classified the withdrawn land; of roughly 68 million acres withdrawn in the first two years, about 36 million were restored after geologists found no workable coal.
The National Conservation Commission reported that Roosevelt had withdrawn over 68,000,000 acres.
political_impact.source: S. Doc. 676, 60th Cong., 2d sess., vol. I, p. 90

political_impact.text: The Coal Lands Act let good-faith farm entrymen take the surface of coal land while the coal was reserved to the United States.
Congress reopened the withdrawn coal lands to entry on the split-estate basis.
The Pickett Act gave the President explicit statutory authority to withdraw public lands.

legacy.text: The Supreme Court described the first withdrawal as 'a departmental order dated July 26, 1906.'
The Supreme Court upheld executive withdrawals made before the Pickett Act, 5 to 3, expressly including the coal withdrawals in the long practice Congress had accepted.
legacy.source: United States v. Midwest Oil Co., 236 U.S. 459, 479 (1915)

legacy.text: The Mineral Leasing Act set up the federal leasing system for coal, oil, gas and other minerals that still governs the mineral estate of the public lands.
